title: The calendar server with too many keys
scenario:
You are an IT risk analyst at a recruitment agency with 150 consultants. The team wants its AI assistant to read consultants' calendars and suggest interview slots. A third-party company offers a remote MCP server for the calendar system.

The IT lead filled in a request form and asks you to review it before go-live. The exhibit shows the form.
exhibit:
MCP server request form (made-up example data)

Server: "CalendarPro MCP", run by a third-party company
Use case: read calendars, suggest interview slots

Tools on the server (all switched on)
  list_events            read
  search_events          read
  create_event           write
  delete_all_events      write
  share_calendar_public  write

OAuth scopes requested: read and write ALL calendars
Approval setting: never ask ("saves time for consultants")
Data: candidate names and interview notes appear in events
AI vendor contract: Zero Data Retention (ZDR) agreed
IT note: "ZDR covers everything, so the server's own data
terms don't matter."
Logging: none

questions.prompt: Which change to the tools fits the vendors' guidance best?

options.text: Keep all five tools on; the model only calls a tool when the user asks for it.
options.explanation: The model decides when to call tools. Both vendors provide tool limits so that unneeded tools can't be called at all.

options.text: Turn on only the read tools the use case needs, and switch off delete and share.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's allowed_tools and Anthropic's allowlist and denylist do this. Anthropic's page recommends denylisting write or destructive tools for read-only assistants.

options.text: Rename delete_all_events to a safer name, so the model is less likely to call it.
options.explanation: A new name doesn't remove the power. The tool can still delete events if it is called.

options.text: Add a line to the prompt: "never delete or share calendars", and keep the tools on.
options.explanation: A prompt line is not a control, and hidden instructions could override it. Switching the tools off removes the risk.

questions.prompt: The server asks for "read and write ALL calendars". What should the review say?

options.text: Accept it: a server needs full access, or OAuth sign-in will fail.
options.explanation: Anthropic's Claude Code page shows you can pin the scopes to an approved subset, even when the server asks for more.

options.text: Accept it, but change the account password every month instead.
options.explanation: A new password doesn't reduce what the access token can do. Scopes do that.

options.text: Reject OAuth and share one consultant's username and password with the server instead.
options.explanation: Shared passwords give full access and no limit. Narrow OAuth scopes are the safer route.

options.text: Grant only the narrowest scope that the use case needs, such as read access to events.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's Claude Code page describes pinning OAuth scopes to a set the security team has approved.

questions.prompt: The IT note says ZDR with the AI vendor covers everything. What is accurate?

options.text: Data sent to the MCP server follows that server's retention terms, so review those too.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's data controls page says MCP servers are third-party services with their own retention policies. Anthropic's MCP connector page says the connector is not covered by ZDR.

options.text: ZDR covers the server too, because the server is reached through the AI vendor's API calls.
options.explanation: The OpenAI docs say data sent to an MCP server follows that server's own retention policies, and the Claude docs say the MCP connector isn't covered by ZDR at all.

options.text: ZDR doesn't matter here, because calendar events never contain personal data.
options.explanation: The exhibit says candidate names and interview notes appear in events.

options.text: ZDR means the server must delete every event after each request, so data is safe.
options.explanation: ZDR is an agreement with the AI vendor. It sets no rules for a third-party server.

questions.prompt: Approval is set to "never ask" and there is no logging. What fits the guidance in the OpenAI docs best?

options.text: Keep "never ask"; approvals are only needed for servers built by your own team.
options.explanation: The guide says the opposite: approvals matter most for third-party servers you don't yet trust.

options.text: Keep "never ask" but add logging, so mistakes can be undone afterwards.
options.explanation: Logs help you find problems, but a deleted calendar or a public share has already happened. Write actions need approval first.

options.text: Turn approvals on, at least for sensitive actions, and log data sent to the server.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's MCP guide says to require approval for sensitive actions, to skip approvals only once you trust a server, and to log data sent to MCP servers.

options.text: Turn approvals on only for read tools, because reading private data is the main risk.
options.explanation: Reads carry risk, but write tools like delete and share have the most direct effect. The guide asks for approval on sensitive actions.
